why: Every B2B company needs new customers, and most first jobs in sales are prospecting jobs: SDR, BDR or business developer. Companies hire people who can find the right accounts, start real conversations with strangers and book meetings that turn into pipeline, week after week, without burning the market or breaking the rules on personal data.
outcome: explain the B2B sales cycle and the SDR / AE / AM roles, write an ideal customer profile and buyer personas, research accounts and spot buying triggers, write cold e-mails and run cold calls that get answers, use LinkedIn without spamming, build a multichannel sequence that respects GDPR, and work out the activity you need from a meeting or revenue goal.

lessons.title: What SDRs and business developers do: the B2B sales cycle
text: A B2B sale goes through stages: prospecting (finding and contacting the right accounts), discovery (understanding the problem), qualification (is there a real project, a budget, a decision maker, a date?), solution and demo, proposal, negotiation and closing, then onboarding, renewal and expansion. Sales cycles last from a few weeks for a small software subscription to a year or more for a large company deal with several decision makers, a pilot and a purchasing department.

Leads come from two directions. Inbound leads raise their hand themselves: a demo request, a downloaded white paper, a webinar sign-up; marketing qualifies them (marketing qualified lead, MQL) and sales follows up fast. Outbound means the company chooses the accounts it wants and reaches out first, by e-mail, phone and LinkedIn. Outbound is slower and gets more rejections, but it lets you go after the accounts you want instead of waiting for whoever comes.

In many SaaS and tech companies the work is split. The SDR (sales development representative) or BDR (business development representative, often the outbound one) researches accounts, contacts them and books qualified meetings. The AE (account executive) runs discovery, demos, proposals and closes the deal. The AM (account manager), KAM (key account manager) or CSM (customer success manager) looks after existing customers: renewals, upsell, satisfaction. In many French SMEs a single business developer or ingénieur commercial does all of it, from the first call to the signature.

SDRs are measured on outcomes and on activity. Outcomes: meetings booked, meetings held (the prospect actually showed up), meetings accepted by the AE as opportunities (sales accepted lead or SQL, sales qualified lead) and the pipeline value they created. Activity: calls, e-mails, LinkedIn touches, conversations. A typical target reads like “12 qualified meetings held per month”; the variable pay is usually tied to meetings held or opportunities created, not to meetings booked, so that nobody books meetings with the wrong people.

In interviews, hiring managers want to hear that you understand the job is a numbers game played with quality: you will hear “no” most of the time, you need a method to organise your day, and you care whether the meetings you book become real deals.
points: Inbound: the prospect comes to you; outbound: you choose the account and reach out first.
SDR / BDR books qualified meetings; AE closes; AM / KAM / CSM grows and renews existing customers.
A meeting booked is not a meeting held, and a meeting held is not an opportunity: know which one you are paid on.
MQL (marketing qualified), SQL (sales qualified), opportunity: each company defines them; learn its definitions in your first week.

example.code:
SDR monthly scorecard (example)
Target: 12 qualified meetings held / month

Activity        Week 1  Week 2  Week 3  Week 4
New prospects       60      60      55      60
Calls              180     170     160     175
Conversations       14      12      11      15
E-mails sent       210     200     190     205
Meetings booked      4       3       4       5
Meetings held        3       3       3       4
Accepted as opps     2       2       2       3
example.note: 16 booked, 13 held, 9 accepted as opportunities: the target of 12 meetings held is met, and the manager will also look at how many became opportunities.

lessons.title: Ideal customer profile and buyer personas
text: The ideal customer profile (ICP) describes the companies that get the most value from your product and are the best customers for you: they buy faster, stay longer and pay well. It uses firmographics (industry, size in employees or revenue, country, growth), technographics (the tools they already use, for example a CRM or an ERP your product connects to) and situations (they are hiring a sales team, opening sites abroad, under a new regulation). A good ICP is built from your best current customers, not from wishes.

The ICP also says who is out. If customers under 50 employees churn after six months, or one industry always needs a feature you do not have, write it down. A clear “no” saves weeks of prospecting in the wrong place. From the ICP you size the market and tier your accounts: Tier 1 (the best fit, worked by hand with deep research), Tier 2 (good fit, semi-personalised) and Tier 3 (possible fit, lighter touch).

Inside each account, several people take part in a B2B purchase. Buyer personas describe the roles you meet: the economic buyer who signs (often a director or the CFO), the champion who wants the change and sells it inside, the users who will use the product every day, and influencers such as IT, security, legal or purchasing who can block the deal. For each persona, note their goals, the numbers they are judged on, their usual problems and the words they use.

Personas turn into messages. A head of sales cares about quota attainment and ramp time of new reps; a CFO about cost, cash and risk; an IT manager about security, integration and the workload for their team. The same product gets three different first lines. Interviewers often ask “who would you target for our product and why?”: answer with an ICP, two or three personas and the problem each one has.
points: ICP = the company that fits; persona = the person inside it.
Build the ICP from your best customers (fast to close, retained, profitable), and write down who is out.
Tier accounts: more research and personalisation for Tier 1, lighter touch for Tier 3.
Map the buying group: economic buyer, champion, users, influencers and blockers.
Each persona gets its own problem statement and its own words.

example.code:
ICP - sales onboarding software
Industry:     B2B software, IT services, business services
Size:         100-1,000 employees, sales team of 15+ reps
Country:      France, Belgium, Switzerland
Signals:      hiring 3+ sales reps, new head of sales, recent funding
Tech:         uses Salesforce or HubSpot CRM
Out:          < 50 employees (no budget, churn); retail chains (field teams)

Persona: VP Sales / Head of Sales
Judged on:    team quota attainment, ramp time of new reps, forecast accuracy
Pains:        new reps take 6+ months to hit quota; managers coach on gut feel
Words:        ramp, quota, pipeline, coaching, enablement
Role in deal: economic buyer (budget owner)
example.note: One page per persona is enough. Update it every quarter with what you hear on calls.

lessons.title: Account research, buying triggers and the target list
text: Before contacting an account, spend a few minutes finding a reason to contact it now. A buying trigger is an event that makes your offer more relevant: a funding round (money to spend and growth targets to hit), hiring (ten sales job ads mean onboarding problems soon), a new leader (new directors usually review their tools and suppliers in their first months), an expansion (new country, new site, acquisition) or a new regulation (for example the French e-invoicing reform, NIS2 for cybersecurity or CSRD for sustainability reporting). Bad news can be a trigger too: a lost customer, a profit warning, a security incident.

Where to look: LinkedIn and LinkedIn Sales Navigator (filters by industry, size, role, recent job changes, company growth), the company website (news, case studies, careers page), job boards, press and trade media, and for listed companies the annual report and results presentations, which say in the management’s own words what their priorities and problems are. For French companies, registry data on Pappers or Societe.com gives revenue, headcount bands and directors.

Turn research into a target list. Start from the ICP filters, remove current customers, open deals and companies that asked not to be contacted, then add the people (personas) in each account with verified contact data. Data enrichment tools find professional e-mails and phone numbers; check them, because a high bounce rate hurts your e-mail deliverability. Keep the list in the CRM, not in a private spreadsheet, so that colleagues see who is being worked.

Research has to stay proportionate. For a Tier 1 account, fifteen minutes on the annual report and the leader’s recent posts is well spent. For Tier 3, one relevant fact about the segment is enough. A common mistake of new SDRs is to research for an hour and then send nothing; another is to send 500 identical e-mails with no reason at all. The goal is one true, specific reason to talk, written in one sentence.
points: Trigger = a recent event that makes your offer relevant now: funding, hiring, new leader, expansion, regulation.
Annual reports and results presentations tell you the priorities in the company’s own words.
Clean the list: no current customers, no open deals, no one who opted out; verify e-mails.
Research depth follows the tier: deep for Tier 1, light for Tier 3.
Write the reason to reach out in one sentence before you write the message.

example.code:
Account: Acme Logistics (fictional) - Tier 1
Fit:        420 employees, freight software, HubSpot CRM, France + Spain
Triggers:   - Series B raised 2 months ago, plan to "double the sales team"
            - 9 open sales job ads (Paris, Madrid)
            - New VP Sales (Claire D.) joined 6 weeks ago from a competitor
Contacts:   Claire D. - VP Sales (economic buyer)
            Marc L.   - Sales enablement manager (likely champion)
Angle:      9 new reps to onboard in 2 countries; how fast can they ramp?
First line: "Saw you are hiring 9 reps across Paris and Madrid after the Series B."
example.note: Three facts, two people and one angle: enough for a relevant first touch.

lessons.title: Cold e-mails that get answers
text: A cold e-mail competes with dozens of other messages and is read on a phone in a few seconds. What works is relevance, brevity and one clear ask. A simple structure: a first line about them (the trigger or an observation), the problem you see in companies like theirs, one line of proof (a similar customer and a result), and one low-friction question. Aim for about 50 to 120 words, plain text, no attachment, no big signature with images.

The subject line only has to get the e-mail opened without misleading: short, specific and honest, such as “ramp time for the 9 new reps” or “question about Madrid”. Fake “Re:” or “Fwd:” subjects and false urgency get opens but destroy trust and your domain’s reputation. The ask is usually an interest question (“Worth a 15-minute chat?”, “Is this a priority this quarter?”) rather than a link to your calendar in the first e-mail: it is easier to answer yes.

Bad cold e-mails talk about the seller: “We are the leading platform…”, three paragraphs of features, a 30-minute demo request, “I hope this e-mail finds you well”. Good ones talk about the reader, use their words and could only have been sent to them. A useful test before sending: would this e-mail still make sense if I sent it to a random company? If yes, it is not personal enough.

Deliverability decides whether the e-mail lands in the inbox at all. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC on the sending domain, warm up new mailboxes slowly, many teams send prospecting from a secondary domain to protect the main one, keep daily volumes per mailbox modest, verify addresses to keep bounces low, and make opting out easy. Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require authentication from bulk senders and ask them to keep spam complaints below 0.3 %. Do not judge an e-mail on its open rate: privacy features such as Apple Mail Privacy Protection make opens unreliable. Judge it on replies, and on positive replies.
points: Structure: first line about them, problem, proof, one ask.
Short (about 50-120 words), plain text, one question that is easy to answer.
Honest subject lines: no fake Re:, no false urgency.
Deliverability: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, warmed-up mailboxes, verified addresses, easy opt-out.
Measure reply rate and positive reply rate, not opens.

example.code:
BAD
Subject: Partnership opportunity!!
Hi, I hope this e-mail finds you well. We are the leading AI-powered
sales enablement platform trusted by 500+ companies. Our features include
[...] Can we book a 30-minute demo this week? Here is my calendar link.

GOOD
Subject: ramp time for the 9 new reps
Hi Claire,
Saw you are hiring 9 reps across Paris and Madrid after the Series B.
When teams double that fast, new reps often take 6+ months to close
their first deals, and managers end up coaching on gut feel.
NordFret cut their ramp from 7 to 4 months with us last year.
Is ramp time on your list for this quarter?
Thomas
(Not relevant? Just reply "no" and I will not write again.)
example.note: The good version is 70 words: a trigger, a problem in her words, one proof and one question. The last line gives an easy opt-out.

lessons.title: Cold calls: opener, reason, questions, meeting
text: A cold call interrupts someone, so the first seconds decide everything. A common structure: greet and say who you are, acknowledge the interruption and ask for a short permission (“It’s a cold call, can I take 30 seconds to tell you why I’m calling, and you tell me if it’s worth continuing?”), give the reason in one or two sentences tied to a problem or a trigger, ask an open question, listen, and if there is interest, book a meeting with a precise time and send the invitation while still on the line.

The reason for the call is a problem statement, not a pitch: “I work with heads of sales who are hiring fast; most tell me new reps take too long to close their first deals. How are you handling that with the nine new hires?” Then listen and ask one or two follow-up questions. The goal of a cold call is not to sell the product; it is to earn the next step, usually a 20 to 30 minute discovery meeting with the AE or with you.

Most calls end on a brush-off, a quick reflex to end the call: “Send me an e-mail”, “Not interested”, “We already have a supplier”, “No budget”, “Call me back in six months”. Treat it as a reflex, not a final answer: acknowledge it, then ask one short question. “Sure, I will. So that it’s useful, what should it focus on: onboarding speed or coaching?” or “Makes sense, most of our customers had a supplier too. What would you change about it if you could?” If the answer is still no, thank them and leave politely: a respectful end keeps the door open.

Practical habits: call in blocks (one or two hours with no e-mail), prepare the first line for each account, stand up and smile (it changes your voice), take notes in the CRM straight after each call, and listen to your recordings or to top colleagues’ calls. Connect rates are low, so persistence across days and times matters, but always respect a clear “please do not call me again”.
points: Opener → permission → reason → open question → listen → book the meeting.
The aim of the call is the next step, not the sale.
Brush-off: acknowledge, ask one question, then accept a real no politely.
Book a precise slot and send the invitation during the call.
Call in focused blocks and log notes in the CRM right away.

example.code:
Rep:      Hi Claire, Thomas from RampUp. It's a cold call - can I take
          30 seconds to tell you why I'm calling, then you decide?
Prospect: ...OK, quickly.
Rep:      I saw you're hiring 9 reps after the Series B. Heads of sales
          in that spot often tell me new hires take 6+ months to ramp.
          How are you planning their onboarding?
Prospect: Honestly, just send me an e-mail.
Rep:      Happy to. So it's useful - is the bigger worry the time to
          first deal, or coaching them across two countries?
Prospect: Time to first deal. The last hires took forever.
Rep:      Then a 20-minute look at how NordFret cut that is worth it.
          Thursday 10:00 or Friday 14:00?
Prospect: Friday 14:00.
Rep:      Done, invitation sent now with a two-line agenda.
example.note: The brush-off ("send me an e-mail") was acknowledged, then one question turned it into a real conversation and a meeting.

lessons.title: LinkedIn and social selling
text: Social selling means using social networks, mostly LinkedIn in B2B, to be found, build credibility and start conversations with the right people, rather than to blast messages. Prospects will look at your profile after your e-mail or call, so it has to work for them: a clear photo, a headline about the problem you solve for customers (“Helping sales teams ramp new reps faster”) rather than “Top SDR, crushing quota”, an About section written for the buyer, and a few useful posts.

Content builds familiarity before you ask for anything. You do not need to be an influencer: share what you learn from customers, comment usefully on your prospects’ posts, congratulate a new leader on the job, repost a customer success with a short insight. A thoughtful comment on a prospect’s post is often a better first touch than a message.

Connection requests: personalise them or send none at all, never pitch in the note. A short reason works: “Saw your post on onboarding sales hires across countries; I work on the same topic. Happy to connect.” Pitching right after someone accepts (often called pitch-slapping) gets ignored or reported. Start a conversation, share something useful, and ask for a meeting only when there is a sign of interest.

LinkedIn Sales Navigator helps with targeting (lead and account lists, alerts on job changes and company news) and LinkedIn gives a Social Selling Index (SSI) score; treat it as a rough guide, not a goal. Respect the platform’s limits on invitations and automation, and remember that what you post is public and attached to your employer’s name.
points: Profile for the buyer: headline about the customer’s problem, not about you.
Comment and share useful insights before asking for anything.
Personalised connection note, no pitch; never pitch right after acceptance.
Sales Navigator: lists, saved searches and alerts on job changes and company news.
Respect LinkedIn’s limits on invitations and automation tools.

example.code:
Headline (before): SDR @RampUp | Top performer | Closing machine
Headline (after):  I help sales leaders ramp new reps faster | Onboarding & coaching

Connection note:
"Hi Marc, your post on onboarding reps across Paris and Madrid was spot on
- especially the point about shadowing. I work with enablement teams on the
same problem. Happy to connect."

After acceptance (no pitch):
"Thanks Marc. We published a short checklist on the first 30 days of a new
rep - want me to send it?"
example.note: Every message gives something or asks a real question; the meeting request comes later, when he shows interest.

lessons.title: Multichannel sequences, tools and GDPR
text: A sequence (or cadence) is a planned series of touches to one prospect across channels over a few weeks: for example eight to twelve touches over three to four weeks, mixing e-mail, phone and LinkedIn. One message rarely gets an answer; a well-spaced sequence where each touch adds something new (a different angle, a case study, a useful resource) gets many more. The last step is often a polite “break-up” e-mail that closes the loop.

Personalisation is organised in tiers. Tier 1 accounts get fully written messages and calls based on deep research; Tier 2 get a persona template with a personalised first line and trigger; Tier 3 get a well-targeted segment message. Sales engagement tools run the sequences, schedule tasks and stop a sequence automatically when the prospect replies: Lemlist, Apollo and La Growth Machine are common in France, with Outreach, Salesloft and HubSpot sequences in larger teams; enrichment tools find contact data. Tools amplify what you put in: a bad message sent automatically to 2,000 people is 2,000 bad impressions.

In France and the EU, prospecting uses personal data, so GDPR applies. For B2B e-mail, the CNIL allows contacting a professional at their work address without prior consent when the message relates to their job (selling sales software to a head of sales, not a holiday offer), provided the person is informed and can object easily and free of charge at any time. Each message says who you are and gives a simple way to opt out; opt-outs go on a suppression list that every tool and colleague respects. Prospect data is kept only as long as needed: the CNIL’s reference is three years after the last contact from the prospect.

For calls, consumers are protected by stricter rules: since 11 August 2026 a company may only cold-call a consumer who has given prior consent (law of 30 June 2025; the Bloctel opt-out list has ended). Calling a professional about their job is B2B prospecting, but the person can still object, and you must stop when asked. Collect only useful data, tell people where you got their details if they ask, and follow your company’s rules: the data protection officer or legal team has the final word, and fines and lost reputation cost far more than one meeting.
points: Sequence = planned multichannel touches over weeks; each one adds something new.
Personalisation tiers: Tier 1 fully custom, Tier 2 template + custom first line, Tier 3 segment message.
Tools (Lemlist, Apollo, La Growth Machine, Outreach, Salesloft) stop the sequence when the prospect replies.
B2B e-mail in France: related to the person’s job, sender identified, easy opt-out honoured everywhere.
Keep prospect data only as long as needed (CNIL: three years after the last contact from the prospect).

example.code:
Sequence "New VP Sales - Tier 2" (15 working days)
Day 1   E-mail 1      Trigger + problem + interest question
Day 1   LinkedIn      View profile, personalised connection note (no pitch)
Day 3   Call 1        Opener + reason; voicemail referring to e-mail
Day 5   E-mail 2      Same thread: customer story (NordFret, ramp 7 -> 4 months)
Day 8   Call 2        Different time of day
Day 10  LinkedIn      Comment on a post or send a useful resource
Day 12  E-mail 3      New angle: coaching across two countries
Day 15  E-mail 4      Break-up: "Should I close the file?" + opt-out line
Rule: any reply -> sequence stops, rep answers by hand
example.note: Eight touches on three channels; every e-mail carries an opt-out line and the tool stops at the first reply.

lessons.title: The numbers: from activity to pipeline
text: Prospecting is a funnel: prospects contacted → replies (or conversations) → meetings booked → meetings held → opportunities → won deals. Each step has a conversion rate, and multiplying them shows what activity a goal needs. If you know your rates, you can plan your week instead of hoping. Reply rate = replies / prospects contacted; meeting rate = meetings / prospects contacted; and so on.

Work backwards from the goal. Suppose a quarterly target of 120,000 EUR of new business, an average deal of 8,000 EUR, a 25 % win rate on opportunities and 50 % of meetings held becoming opportunities: you need 15 deals, so 60 opportunities, so 120 meetings held in the quarter. If 40 % of replies become meetings and 8 % of prospects reply, a monthly goal of 12 meetings needs 12 / (0.08 × 0.4) = 375 new prospects in sequence each month.

Improve one rate at a time with A/B tests: two subject lines, two first lines or two calls to action, sent at random to similar prospects in the same week. Change one thing only, compare reply rates (or positive replies), and wait for enough volume: with 100 e-mails per variant, a difference of two or three replies is mostly noise. Relative lift = rate of B / rate of A − 1.

A weekly review keeps the machine honest. Look at activity (did I do what I planned?), conversion at each step (where does it leak?), the quality of meetings (how many held, how many accepted as opportunities) and a few listened calls or read replies. Then decide one change for next week: new trigger list, new opener, more call blocks. Managers trust reps who know their numbers and explain them without excuses.
points: Funnel: prospects → replies → meetings booked → held → opportunities → won.
Work backwards: revenue target / deal size / win rate / meeting-to-opportunity rate = meetings needed.
A/B test one variable, judge on replies, and wait for enough volume.
Relative lift = rate B / rate A − 1.
Weekly review: activity, conversion per step, meeting quality, one change.

example.code:
A1: Prospects   B1: Replies   C1: Meetings held   D1: Opportunities
A2: 500         B2: 40        C2: 16              D2: 8

Reply rate                  =B2/A2          -> 8 %
Meeting rate                =C2/A2          -> 3.2 %
Reply to meeting            =C2/B2          -> 40 %
Meeting to opportunity      =D2/C2          -> 50 %
Prospects for 12 meetings   =12/(C2/A2)     -> 375
example.note: Each ratio divides the next step by the step before; the last line works backwards from a goal of 12 meetings.

lessons.title: Field and SMB sales: territory, visits, trade shows and quotes
text: Many French sales offers are not SaaS jobs: “commercial terrain”, “technico-commercial”, “chargé d’affaires” or “attaché commercial” sell equipment, supplies, maintenance, building works or industrial parts to small and mid-size businesses, craftsmen, shops, factories and local authorities on a territory (secteur) of a few départements. The same person usually hunts new accounts and farms existing ones, from the first call to the signed quote and sometimes to the payment. The territory starts with account tiering: rank accounts by revenue or potential into A, B and C. A few A accounts usually weigh most of the revenue (the Pareto rule of thumb), so they get the most visits, for example every month; B accounts every quarter; C accounts by phone and e-mail, with a visit when there is a project. Add a list of high-potential prospects, tiered the same way.

Plan tours (tournées) by zone, not by mood: split the territory into zones, give each zone its day, fix the important appointments by phone a week or two ahead, then fill the gaps with nearby prospect or customer visits instead of zig-zagging across the map. Many field reps keep one day, or two half-days, a week at the desk for quotes, calls and the CRM. Prepare each visit in five minutes: CRM history, last orders, open quotes, unpaid invoices, and one objective (a quote for the new line, a trial, meeting the production manager). During the visit, thank them, say how long you will stay, ask what has changed, look at the site or the installation, present the one solution that fits what you heard and leave with a dated next step.

SMB owners decide alone, are busy and value someone reliable who comes back. Walk-ins (visiting without an appointment) work for shops, trade counters and workshops near your appointments: ask for the owner, introduce yourself in two sentences, and if it is not a good time ask when to come back rather than pitching to whoever is at the counter. For owners who are often away, a short phone call to book a 20-minute visit works better: give a reason linked to their business (a new regulation, a breakdown risk, a product that saves them time) and propose two precise slots. Writing down the owner’s name, mobile and opening hours is personal data: keep it to what is useful, in the CRM, and stop if they ask you to.

Trade shows (salons professionnels) concentrate prospects in two or three days, but only pay off when they are worked before, during and after. Before: list the target accounts that exhibit or visit, invite customers and prospects with your stand number, book meetings on the stand and agree three or four qualification questions with the team. During: qualify each visitor in a minute or two (need, timing, role in the decision), capture the lead with a badge scan or a form and a note of what was said, and agree a next step. After: send every lead a follow-up that recalls your conversation within days, while they still remember you, call the hot leads first, put everyone in the CRM, and compare the leads, quotes and orders with what the show cost. Badge scans are personal data: the follow-up says who you are and offers an easy opt-out, as in the rest of this course.

In field and SMB sales the quote (devis) is where the deal is won or lost. It lists the goods or services, quantities and unit prices before tax (HT), any discount, the net total HT, VAT (20 % standard rate in France; some goods and works have reduced rates) and the total including VAT (TTC), plus the delivery time, the payment terms (between companies the legal maximum is 60 days from the invoice date, or 45 days end of month if agreed), the validity date and a space for “bon pour accord” and the signature. Know your margin before you discount it: on a price of 100 with a cost of 70, a 10 % discount turns a margin of 30 into 20, a third of it gone. Follow every quote up a few days after sending it (received? questions? decision date?) and again before it expires. Log visits and quotes from your phone in the CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot, or Sellsy and Axonaut, common in French SMEs) the same day. Managers look at visits per week, new accounts opened, quotes sent, the quote conversion rate (quotes signed / quotes sent, in number and in value), the average basket (revenue / number of orders), the margin rate and revenue against target.
points: ABC tiering: A accounts weigh most and get the most visits; C accounts are worked by phone and e-mail.
Tour by zone: one zone per day, key appointments fixed ahead, gaps filled with nearby visits.
Visit: CRM history before, one objective, a dated next step, report in the CRM the same day.
Trade show: book meetings before, qualify and capture each lead, follow up within days.
Quote: unit price HT, discount, net HT, VAT 20 %, TTC, delivery, payment terms, validity; follow it up.
Quote conversion = quotes signed / quotes sent; average basket = revenue / orders; margin rate = margin / net price.

example.code:
A1: Item                 B1: Qty   C1: Unit price HT   D1: Line total HT
A2: Pallet racking bay   B2: 12    C2: 450             D2: =B2*C2        -> 5,400
A3: Installation (day)   B3: 2     C3: 600             D3: =B3*C3        -> 1,200

Total HT before discount   D4: =SUM(D2:D3)    -> 6,600
Discount 5 %               D5: =D4*5%         -> 330
Net total HT               D6: =D4-D5         -> 6,270
VAT 20 %                   D7: =D6*20%        -> 1,254
Total incl. VAT (TTC)      D8: =D6+D7         -> 7,524

Cost HT (goods + fitter)   D9: 4,800
Margin HT                  D10: =D6-D9        -> 1,470
Margin rate on net price   D11: =D10/D6       -> 23.4 %

Valid 30 days. Delivery 3 weeks after signed quote. Payment 30 days from invoice date.
example.note: The discount comes off the HT total, VAT is added last, and the margin is computed on the net HT price: a 5 % discount here cost 330 EUR of margin out of 1,800.

A low-friction question such as “Is this a priority this quarter?”
SPF, DKIM, DMARC
E-mail authentication records that protect deliverability
Positive reply rate
Interested replies / prospects contacted: better than open rate
Social selling
Using LinkedIn to be found, build credibility and start conversations, not to blast messages
Pitch-slapping
Pitching right after a connection is accepted: avoid it
Permission opener
Acknowledge the interruption and ask for 30 seconds to explain why you are calling
Reason for the call
A problem statement or trigger, not a product pitch
Brush-off
A reflex to end the call (“send me an e-mail”): acknowledge, ask one question
Next step
The goal of the call: a precise meeting slot, invitation sent during the call
Sequence (cadence)
Planned multichannel touches over a few weeks, stopped at the first reply
Break-up e-mail
The polite last step that closes the loop
Personalisation tiers
Fully custom / template + custom first line / segment message
B2B e-mail rule (CNIL)
Allowed to a work address without prior consent if related to the job, with an easy opt-out
Suppression list
Everyone who opted out, respected by every tool and colleague
Reply rate
Replies / prospects contacted
Meeting rate
Meetings / prospects contacted
Meetings needed
Revenue target / deal size / win rate / meeting-to-opportunity rate
Prospects needed
Meetings goal / (reply rate × reply-to-meeting rate)
Relative lift
Rate B / rate A − 1
ABC accounts
A: the few accounts that weigh most, visited most often; B: regular visits; C: phone and e-mail
Tour (tournée)
Visits grouped by zone, key appointments fixed ahead, gaps filled with nearby visits
Quote (devis)
Lines HT, discount, net HT, VAT, TTC, delivery, payment terms, validity, “bon pour accord”
HT / TTC
Before tax / including VAT; French standard VAT rate 20 %; discounts apply to HT
Quote conversion rate
Quotes signed / quotes sent, in number and in value
Average basket
Revenue / number of orders
Margin rate
Margin / net selling price HT (French “taux de marque”); margin / cost is the markup (“taux de marge”)

pitfalls: Sending the same generic e-mail to hundreds of people with no reason to contact them now: low replies, spam complaints and a damaged domain.
Pitching the product in the first seconds of a cold call or in a LinkedIn connection note instead of earning the next step.
Taking the first brush-off as a final answer, or the opposite: insisting after a clear “please do not contact me again”.
Booking meetings with people who are not in the ICP or have no role in the decision: they do not show up or never become opportunities.
Judging e-mails on open rates, or declaring an A/B test winner after a handful of replies.
Ignoring GDPR basics: no sender identification, no opt-out, opt-outs not shared between tools, data kept forever.
Keeping prospect notes outside the CRM, so colleagues contact the same people twice.
Giving a discount on the spot without knowing the margin or getting anything in return, then sending the quote and never following it up.

exercises.q: A prospect accepted a first meeting booked by the SDR. In a typical SaaS sales team, who runs the discovery and later closes the deal?
options: The SDR who booked the meeting
exercises.answer: The SDR books qualified meetings, the AE runs discovery, demo, proposal and closing, and the CSM or account manager looks after the customer after the signature. In many SMEs one business developer does all of it.

exercises.q: A sequence went to 400 prospects and got 28 replies. What is the reply rate, in percent?
exercises.answer: 28 / 400 = 0.07, a 7 % reply rate. Then look at how many of these replies are positive: a reply saying “stop” counts as a reply but not as a lead.

exercises.q: In E2, the reply rate of the sequence: all replies, across the three steps, divided by the prospects contacted.
exercises.hint: Add the replies of the three steps, then divide by the number of prospects.
exercises.explain: (14 + 9 + 4) / 450 = 27 / 450 = 0.06, a 6 % reply rate. Divide by prospects, not by e-mails sent: each prospect got up to three e-mails, so dividing by e-mails would make the sequence look worse than it is.

exercises.q: In E2, the number of meetings held needed in the quarter to reach the new-business target.
exercises.hint: Target / deal size = deals; deals / win rate = opportunities; opportunities / meeting-to-opportunity rate = meetings.
exercises.explain: 120000 / 8000 = 15 deals; 15 / 0.25 = 60 opportunities; 60 / 0.5 = 120 meetings held in the quarter, about 40 a month for the team. =A2/(B2*C2*D2) gives the same result.

exercises.q: In D2, the number of new prospects to put in sequence each month to hold the meeting goal.
exercises.hint: Each prospect gives reply rate × reply-to-meeting rate meetings. Divide the goal by that.
exercises.explain: 0.08 × 0.4 = 0.032 meetings per prospect, so 12 / 0.032 = 375 prospects a month, about 19 per working day. Raising the reply rate to 10 % would bring it down to 300: better messages save activity.

exercises.q: In B6, the conversion of the sequence from prospect to opportunity.
exercises.hint: Opportunities divided by the prospects at the top of the funnel.
exercises.explain: 9 / 500 = 0.018, so 1.8 % of the prospects became opportunities. The step rates multiply to the same number: 45/500 × 18/45 × 9/18 = 0.09 × 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.018.

exercises.q: In D3, the relative lift in reply rate of subject line B over subject line A.
rows: B: ramp time for the 9 new reps
exercises.hint: Reply rate of B divided by the reply rate of A, minus 1.
exercises.explain: A: 15 / 250 = 6 %; B: 24 / 250 = 9.6 %; 9.6 / 6 − 1 = 0.6, a 60 % relative lift (3.6 points). With only 250 e-mails each, the gap is 9 replies: promising, but repeat the test on a new batch before rolling B out everywhere.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a cold call in order.
steps: Greet and say who you are
Acknowledge the interruption and ask for 30 seconds
Give the reason for the call: a problem or a trigger
Ask an open question and listen
Handle the brush-off with one question
Book a precise slot and send the invitation during the call
exercises.answer: Opener → permission → reason → question → brush-off handling → meeting. The goal is the next step, not the sale.

exercises.q: Sort these cold e-mail lines into good and bad.

groups.name: Good
items: Saw you are hiring 9 reps across Paris and Madrid after the Series B.
Is ramp time on your list for this quarter?
NordFret cut their ramp from 7 to 4 months with us last year.
Not relevant? Just reply “no” and I will not write again.

groups.name: Bad
items: I hope this e-mail finds you well.
We are the leading AI-powered platform trusted by 500+ companies.
Here is my calendar link: book 30 minutes this week.
Subject: Re: our conversation (when there was none)

exercises.answer: Good lines are about the reader (trigger, their problem), give proof and ask one easy question, with an opt-out. Bad lines are filler, talk about the seller, ask for too much too soon, or mislead.

exercises.q: Match each buying trigger with the best angle for a first message (you sell sales onboarding and coaching software).
pairs: Series B raised, plan to double the sales team
Getting many new reps productive quickly
New VP Sales joined six weeks ago
Help with a first-90-days plan and quick wins for the team
Onboarding and coaching reps in two countries and two languages
Quarterly results mention missed sales targets
Raising the share of reps who hit quota
exercises.answer: A trigger gives the reason to write now; the angle links it to the problem your product solves for that persona.

exercises.q: You cold-call the head of sales of a mid-size company that is hiring reps.

steps.text: She picks up: “Yes?” What do you say first?

choices.label: “Hi, Thomas from RampUp. It’s a cold call, can I take 30 seconds to tell you why I’m calling, then you decide?”
choices.feedback: Honest and short: she knows what is happening and keeps control, which lowers her guard.

choices.label: “Hi, how are you today?”
choices.feedback: A stranger asking how she is sounds like a script and wastes the few seconds you have.

choices.label: Start presenting the product and its main features
choices.feedback: A pitch before any reason or question gets an immediate “not interested”.

steps.text: After your reason, she says: “Just send me an e-mail.”

choices.label: “Sure. So it’s useful, is the bigger issue the time to first deal or coaching across two sites?”
choices.feedback: You accept, then ask one question that turns the reflex into a conversation.

choices.label: “OK, bye” and hang up
choices.feedback: You gave up on a reflex answer; the e-mail will probably not be read.

choices.label: “I only need 30 more minutes, it will be worth it, I promise”
choices.feedback: Pushing harder after a brush-off feels like pressure and ends the call.

steps.text: She answers: “We already work with a training company.”

choices.label: “Makes sense, most of our customers did too. What would you improve about it if you could?”
choices.feedback: You respect her choice and look for a gap; her answer tells you if there is a real reason to meet.

choices.label: “They are much worse than us, you should switch”
choices.feedback: Criticising her current supplier criticises her decision.

choices.label: “Then there is nothing I can do for you”
choices.feedback: An existing supplier is common; one question would have shown whether there is a gap.

steps.text: She says the new hires take too long to close their first deal. Next step?

choices.label: Propose two precise slots for a 20-minute meeting and send the invitation while on the phone
choices.feedback: A concrete next step with a date: the purpose of the call.

choices.label: “I’ll call you back sometime next month”
choices.feedback: No date, no meeting: the interest will fade.

choices.label: Send the full price list straight away
choices.feedback: Prices without discovery turn the talk into a cost comparison too early.

exercises.answer: Permission opener, a reason tied to her situation, one question after each brush-off, then a precise meeting. If she clearly says no, thank her and stop.

exercises.q: Under GDPR as applied by the CNIL in France, when can you send a prospecting e-mail to a professional address without prior consent?
options: Never: B2B prospecting e-mails always need prior consent
When the message relates to the person’s job and they can easily object to further messages
Any time, as long as the address was found on LinkedIn
Only if the company has signed up to a national opt-in list
exercises.answer: B2B e-mails to a work address are allowed without prior consent if the offer relates to the person’s profession, the person is informed and can object easily and free of charge. The consumer phone rules (prior consent since 11 August 2026, which replaced the Bloctel list) are a separate matter, not a rule for B2B e-mail.

exercises.q: Write a 3-step outbound sequence (two e-mails and one call, with days) for the VP Sales of a fictional company that just raised a Series B and is hiring 9 reps. You sell sales onboarding software. Keep each e-mail under 100 words.
exercises.answer:
Day 1, e-mail 1. Subject: ramp time for the 9 new reps. “Hi Claire, saw you are hiring 9 reps across Paris and Madrid after the Series B. When teams grow that fast, new reps often take 6+ months to close their first deals. NordFret cut their ramp from 7 to 4 months with us. Is ramp time a priority this quarter? Thomas. (Not relevant? Reply “no” and I will not write again.)”
Day 3, call. “Hi Claire, Thomas from RampUp, it’s a cold call, can I take 30 seconds to say why? … I wrote about the 9 new reps: how are you planning their first 90 days?” If voicemail: 20 seconds, one reason, mention the e-mail.
Day 6, e-mail 2 (same thread). “Claire, one more idea: NordFret’s managers used one shared scorecard to coach reps in two countries, which helped new hires reach their first deal faster. Happy to show how in 20 minutes, Thursday or Friday?” What makes it good: a real trigger, the persona’s problem, proof, one ask per touch, a new angle each time, an opt-out line, and the sequence stops at the first reply.

exercises.q: In E2, the total including VAT of the quote: quantity × unit price HT, minus the discount, plus VAT.
exercises.hint: Gross HT = quantity × unit price; net HT = gross × (1 − discount); TTC = net × (1 + VAT rate).
exercises.explain: 40 × 85 = 3,400 HT; with 10 % off, 3,400 × 0.9 = 3,060 net HT; with 20 % VAT, 3,060 × 1.2 = 3,672 TTC. The discount always applies to the HT amount, before VAT.

exercises.q: In E2, the visits needed this month to reach the target: orders needed, then quotes, then visits.
exercises.hint: Target / average order = orders; orders / quote conversion = quotes; quotes / quotes per visit = visits.
exercises.explain: 30,000 / 2,500 = 12 orders; 12 / 0.4 = 30 quotes; 30 / 0.5 = 60 visits, about 3 per working day. Raising the quote conversion to 50 % would bring it down to 48 visits: following up quotes saves road time.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a customer visit in order.
steps: Read the account’s CRM history, recent orders and open quotes
Set one objective for the visit and confirm the appointment
Thank them and say how long you will stay
Ask what has changed and look at the site or the installation
Present the one solution that fits what you heard
Agree a dated next step: a quote by Friday, a trial, a demo
Write the visit report in the CRM before the next appointment
exercises.answer: Prepare → objective → open → listen and look → one solution → dated next step → CRM report. A visit without a next step is a courtesy call.

exercises.q: Sort these trade show tasks into before, during and after the show.

groups.name: Before
items: List the target accounts that exhibit or visit and book meetings on the stand
Invite customers and prospects with a short e-mail giving the stand number
Agree three or four qualification questions with the team

groups.name: During
items: Ask each visitor about their need, timing and role in the decision
Scan the badge and note what was said and the next step agreed

groups.name: After
items: Call the hot leads first, within two or three working days
Send each lead a follow-up recalling the conversation, with an opt-out
Compare leads, quotes and orders with the cost of the show

exercises.answer: A show is won before (meetings booked, questions ready), worked during (qualify and capture) and cashed after (fast follow-up, CRM, return on cost).

exercises.q: The owner of a joinery workshop has your quote for a dust extraction system: 8,000 EUR HT, cost 5,440 EUR HT, so a 32 % margin rate.

steps.text: He says: “Give me 15 % off now and I sign today.” What do you do first?

choices.label: Ask what the 15 % is based on: another quote, his budget or a habit
choices.feedback: You learn what the request really is before touching the price; often it is a reflex or a budget, not a better offer.

choices.label: Accept: a signature today is worth it
choices.feedback: 15 % off brings the price to 6,800 and the margin from 2,560 to 1,360 EUR, almost half of it gone in one sentence.

choices.label: “Our prices are fixed, take it or leave it”
choices.feedback: A flat refusal ends the talk; he may sign with someone else who listened.

steps.text: He answers: “The other supplier is 15 % cheaper.”

choices.label: Ask to compare like for like: same power, installation, warranty, delivery time and service
choices.feedback: Quotes often differ on what they include; comparing line by line shows the real gap.

choices.label: Match the price without seeing the other quote
choices.feedback: You pay for a gap you have not checked, and he learns that asking works.

choices.label: Say the other supplier sells poor equipment
choices.feedback: Criticising a competitor criticises his judgement and sounds defensive.

steps.text: The other quote has no installation. His real limit is a budget of 7,600 EUR HT.

choices.label: Offer a trade-off within your authority: 5 % off if he signs this week, keeping installation and warranty
choices.feedback: 7,600 HT keeps a 2,160 EUR margin, and the discount buys something: a fast signature.

choices.label: Give the 15 % anyway to be sure
choices.feedback: He was ready at 7,600: the extra 10 % is margin given away for nothing.

choices.label: Promise 15 % and ask your manager afterwards
choices.feedback: Never promise beyond your authority: if the manager says no, you lose the customer’s trust.

steps.text: He agrees on 7,600 EUR HT. Next step?

choices.label: Send an updated quote with the new price, delivery date and validity, get it signed “bon pour accord” and log it in the CRM
choices.feedback: A written, signed quote protects both sides and feeds the pipeline and the forecast.

choices.label: Shake hands and order the equipment without paperwork
choices.feedback: An oral agreement leaves price, delivery and payment terms open to dispute.

choices.label: Keep the old quote and correct the price on the invoice
choices.feedback: The signed document would not match the deal; the invoice will be contested.

exercises.answer: Find out what the discount request is based on, compare like for like, trade any concession for something (fast signature, volume, payment terms) within your authority, and close with an updated signed quote. Know your margin before you negotiate.

interview.q: Why do you want to be an SDR / business developer?
interview.a: Show that you know what the job is: lots of outreach, many rejections, clear numbers. Give a concrete reason (you like talking to people, learning how businesses work, a measurable job with a career path to AE), and a proof of resilience and organisation: a target you hit, a job with daily objectives, a sport or project where you kept going after setbacks. Mention that you would track your own conversion rates.

interview.q: Who would you target for our product, and how would you find them?
interview.a: Start from their best customers: industry, size, tools, situation. Name two or three personas (the budget owner, the champion, the user) and the problem each has. Then explain the sources: Sales Navigator filters, the careers page and job ads, funding news, annual reports, and the triggers you would watch. Prepare this with real examples from their website before the interview.

interview.q: Write me a cold e-mail for our product, right now.
interview.a: Keep it short and structured: a first line about a specific prospect or trigger, the problem in their words, one proof (a customer result from their website), and one easy question. Under 100 words, honest subject line, opt-out line. Say what you would test next (another first line or call to action) and how you would measure it: replies, not opens.

interview.q: Sell me this pen / Let’s role-play a cold call.
interview.a: Do not pitch features straight away. Open with permission, then ask questions: what they use now, when they last needed one, what bothers them. Link one benefit to what they said and ask for a next step. Handle a brush-off calmly with one question. The interviewer judges your structure, your listening and your calm, not the pen.

interview.q: You need 12 meetings a month. How much activity do you plan?
interview.a: Work backwards with conversion rates and say they are assumptions to check after two weeks. For example with an 8 % reply rate and 40 % of replies becoming meetings: 12 / (0.08 × 0.4) = 375 prospects a month, about 19 new prospects a day in a multichannel sequence, with daily call blocks. Then improve the rates (better targeting, triggers, messages) rather than only adding volume.

interview.q: A prospect says “We already have a supplier.” What do you answer?
interview.a: Acknowledge it as normal, then ask a question that looks for a gap: “Makes sense, most of our customers did too. If you could change one thing about it, what would it be?” or ask when the contract renews. Never criticise the current supplier. If there is no gap, thank them, note the renewal date in the CRM and come back with a reason later.

interview.q: What are the rules for B2B prospecting by e-mail in France?
interview.a: GDPR applies to professional contact data. The CNIL allows e-mails to a work address without prior consent if the offer relates to the person’s job, the sender is identified and the person can opt out easily at any time; opt-outs must be respected across every tool. Collect only useful data, keep it no longer than needed (the CNIL’s reference is three years after the last contact from the prospect) and follow the company’s data protection officer. The stricter phone rules (prior consent since 11 August 2026, replacing Bloctel) concern consumers.

interview.q: You take over a territory of three départements with 150 accounts. How do you organise your week?
interview.a: Rank the accounts A, B, C by revenue and potential in the CRM, then set a visit frequency per class (for example A monthly, B quarterly, C by phone with a visit when there is a project) and add a list of prospects. Split the territory into zones with one day each, book the key appointments a week or two ahead and fill the gaps with nearby visits. Keep time at the desk for quotes, follow-ups and the CRM. Each week check visits, quotes sent and signed, the average basket and the margin against target, and adjust.

interview.q: What goes into a good quote, and what do you do after sending it?
interview.a: Clear lines with quantities and unit prices HT, any discount, the net total HT, VAT (20 % standard rate in France) and the TTC total, delivery time, payment terms (legal maximum between companies: 60 days from the invoice date, or 45 days end of month if agreed), a validity date and the general terms of sale. Before discounting, I check the margin. After sending, I call within a few days to check it arrived and answer questions, ask for the decision date, follow up again before it expires and log every step in the CRM; I track my quote conversion rate in number and value.
